candidates.title: Why Your Company Doesn't Need the Most Expensive AI Model
candidates.author: Nate B Jones
candidates.paywall: video free; companion Executive Briefing paid (AI Executive Circle tier), only intro readable
candidates.what_changed: Argues enterprises now test cheap models against their own requirements and buy the cheapest that passes, so token volume grows while AI spend stays flat (cites Ramp data: near-zero token-spend growth Aug-Sep, total AI spend +1.65% in Oct).
candidates.mechanism: Eval fluency as purchasing power: define good work, compare models on it, route tasks (support, coding) to the cheapest passing tier, use the evidence to negotiate enterprise discounts. Companion post (natesnewsletter.substack.com/p/ai-evals-pricing-power, 2026-11-15) adds a worked example: 5x tokens can leave a $5,000 bill flat via cheaper models/discounts; promises an evals kit (test record, purchase-and-return worksheet, decision prompt) behind the paywall.
candidates.evidence_quality: Commentary. Ramp figures quoted in the free part of the companion post; not checked against Ramp's own release. Chapters and argument from feed description and the post's free intro only; video not watched.
candidates.relevance: High: practical model-selection and procurement argument for teams paying AI bills; ties directly to evals practice.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: New (not in 2026-11-15 issue). Thematically adjacent to prior issue's cost-attribution/model-routing items (Bedrock Switchyard, Cloudflare Spend Management).
candidates.summary: Full video (~17 min per chapters). Watch 05:26 'The math of moving to cheaper models' through 10:12 'Customer support, coding, and model routing'; 16:54 'What I'd want before buying AI' is the checklist. Takeaway: before renewing a frontier-model contract, run your own task evals on a cheaper tier; if it passes, either switch or use the result to negotiate. Not sponsored (description promotes only Nate's own newsletter).

candidates.title: Claude Code 2.1.325
candidates.author: Anthropic
candidates.what_changed: Sandboxed Bash commands now go through the normal permission flow by default (set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true to keep prompt-free behavior, incl. in managed settings). Scheduled tasks and /loop now ask before running a skill that declares allowed-tools or hooks (add Skill(name) to permissions.allow). 'Always allow' in Desktop/IDE/SDK only offers a rule when saving it would actually re-allow the command, so scheduled tasks relying on one can now block. Read-only git in non-project/untrusted repos asks first (use --add-dir). Sandbox refuses writes to .claude settings/skills/agents/hooks in added dirs. Subagents cut off at the output limit are re-asked for the full answer more briefly. CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS now applies to unrecognized claude-* model IDs (gateways). 88 bug fixes incl. a zstd decoding security fix and gateway/Foundry sessions failing with context-length errors instead of compacting.
candidates.mechanism: Permission-model tightening: removes implicit auto-approval paths for sandboxed shell, skills run unattended, and repos outside the trusted set.
candidates.evidence_quality: Primary source (official changelog generated from CHANGELOG.md).
candidates.relevance: High: unattended/scheduled Claude Code setups and CI wrappers may start stalling on prompts after upgrading; the fix is a specific settings key.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: New (no changelogs in 2026-11-15 issue).
candidates.summary: If you run Claude Code unattended (scheduled tasks, /loop, sandboxed CI), check after upgrading to 2.1.325: add sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true and Skill(name) allow rules where you deliberately want prompt-free runs. Gateway users get a fix for context-length failures and can now set context size for custom claude-* IDs.
